utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness, Mr. Tupajic, to the -- oh no, first I have to ask Mr. Registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I come to the next on my programme. Mr. Usher, would you escort the witness into the courtroom. Meanwhile I informed the parties about scheduling. We gave it some thought. For this witness, the Prosecution has taken four hours and 26 minutes. The Judges have taken 40 minutes. On the basis of the 60 per cent guidance, there would be left approximately one hour and 20 minutes. Mr. Stewart, you may use that time. We will grant some additional time to Mr. Krajisnik. We're thinking in terms of approximately 15 minutes. At the same time, we can't go on having fights over how to divide time in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has allowed Mr. Krajisnik to put some additional questions if the witness is cross-examined. That would not under all circumstances exclude to present one or more exhibits to a witness. At the same time, the developments goes in a direction where it's kind of a second cross-examination; that's certainly not what the Chamber had in mind. The Chamber is specifically concerned about the introduction of exhibits that often are not of great assistance to the Chamber and perhaps could be introduced in another way at another moment and also are introduced sometimes in unorderly manner. The Chamber is concerned about this and the Chamber might come up with a kind of ruling on how we'll deal with that rather soon. But for today, it may be clear one hour and 20 minutes left under the 60 per cent guidance and approximately 15 minutes available for Mr. Krajisnik for some additional questions. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I give Your Honour some good news immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- I will come nowhere near using up that allocation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honours will see very soon how far I aim to be away from using up that allocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's good news to the extent that the Chamber wants this trial to be conducted in an orderly and fair way and it's not -- so to that extent it's not specifically good news. It's not the aim of the Chamber to reduce time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I look at it this way, Your Honour, if it's my assessment for the Defence that's all I need, that's got to be good news that that's less than Your Honours had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you understand using less time in cross-examination is not, per se, good news for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We understand each other, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Tupajic, good morning. When you came into the courtroom you were caught --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in a procedural matter. Again, good morning and I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stewart will continue his cross-examination. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your evidence on Tuesday this week you talked about a meeting in Sokolac on the 17th of May, 1992, and you described how it was at the initiative of the association of Serbs from Belgrade who hailed from the Romaninka region and you went on to -- you went on to describe that meeting. You said -- I just want to ask you. There were no -- there were representatives of several municipalities at that meeting. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There were no separate meetings held on that occasion between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic on the one hand and representatives of individual municipalities on the other hand, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tupajic, Mr. Krajisnik will have an opportunity to put some questions to you. Mr. Krajisnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: First of all, good morning, Mr. Tupajic. I'm pleased to see you again after a somewhat longer period of time. You had the opportunity to see the document -- I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I give the document to the registrar just in case we need to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My questions, again to be very easy, and I would ask you to allow for a break between what I say and your answer in order to give the interpreters time to interpret. The document number 1 that you saw, it is the set of instructions from the SDS, or rather the A and B option. Did the Prosecution show you the document that Milovan Bjelica sent to this Tribunal, and it has to do with the origin of that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer to this question I wanted to say good morning to Mr. Krajisnik as well. I believe that I was not shown that document. I don't think I was shown any document that Mr. Bjelica sent or submitted to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could we just keep everything brief. I only have 15 minutes, so let's try and speed things up a bit. Are you aware that in those instructions, if you could just show this set of instructions, I'm just going to indicate one question there. You are option 1 there, of course?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you just refer to page 2 of that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the document, please. Could you please show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the 19th of December document that is -- well, as many copies must be around. It's the last document in this -- could I just have a look at it? That's the one, yes. It may be shown to the witness. Please, page 2 has again been distributed during Mr. Tupajic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Were you called commander of the Crisis Staff or how did people address you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official title of the head of the Crisis Staff was not a commander but the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to refer to page 2 SAO 2598, number 4. To convene and proclaim the Assembly of the Serb people in the municipality made up of representatives of the Serb people at the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Tupajic, is this: Would it be logical for a municipality that -- where you have total majority, absolute majority, to be claimed as a Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I did mention that in my previous interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this document was published in the month of January 1992 in the paper called Slobodna Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution submit this proof or piece of evidence to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did you - and I'm referring to document number 2 here, you don't need to read it now - but are you aware of the fact that there were negotiations going on under this sponsorship, as it were, of Mr. Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that each party submitted their own map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the details, but I know that there was some activity in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you with reference to document 3, policies as of the 19th of March, could you take a look at the maps enclosed here. We've got three maps from three parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Krajisnik, I have one or two questions to you. You asked the witness whether he was aware that the document that's, I take it, the 19th of December document, was published in the month of January 1992. Is this publication in evidence? I'm not quite sure about it. Mr. Tieger, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've certainly seen it before, Your Honour. Whether it's formally in -- I'd be surprised if it's not in as an exhibit somewhere because we have definitely seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I know there has been at least one previous reference, I believe a number of previous references, to such a publication in March of 1992. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: March is not January, so I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, could I say that accords with my recollection that it was March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- my recollection is faulty, but when matched by Mr. Tieger's recollection, I have slightly more confidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see at a later stage whether January or March is -- we'll have a look further upon closing of the evidence in this respect. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, the witness said he has no knowledge about details about these maps. I'll allow you request one or two short questions, but if the witness has no specific knowledge where we dealt extensively with the Cutileiro Plans and where the Chamber has understood what role it plays in the Defence, we'll be hesitant to ask the witness about what he is not specifically aware of. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to enclose those three maps and use them as exhibits, and I'm going to ask just one question in relation to the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to take a look at the maps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I mean now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the maps in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There must be maps in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, Witness Tupajic, have a look at tab 3. Mr. Krajisnik, there are not three maps, there are as a matter of fact five maps. So would you please identify -- I take it you are referring to the second page where three maps appear on one page. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do the relevant document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what these maps refer to. You can read it at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that demarcation maps of BH submitted by SDS, SDA, and HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now I come to my actual question. As to the first map, could you identify what party submitted that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's clear what's happening. The witness has no particular information about the negotiations about these documents and now he's being asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you have any idea what maps were submitted by whom or by what party?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would ask independent of his current reading of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes. Were you aware, apart from what you see at this moment, who submitted what kind of maps during negotiations and whether -- have you ever seen those maps before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do remember that those talks were being held and that some maps existed and that all three parties had their proposals. But I might have been aware of some of the details at the time but I've quite frankly forgotten it. I would need some more time to study the maps and then I might be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One question to the parties: Who submitted what maps during the Cutileiro negotiations seems to be a matter one might not be able to agree on. I mean, if one party finds that of importance, is it so difficult to -- if the -- Mr. Krajisnik would like the Chamber to look at those maps to reach an agreement upon what maps are used at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quite agree it's an appropriate matter for such discussion and it seems like a matter that can be resolved in precisely the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even without asking questions to a witness who doesn't seem to be -- know a lot about the matter. Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand you would like to establish who used what maps during the Cutileiro negotiations. There are perfect ways to establish that. The Chamber does not oppose in any way. But it is not of great use to ask that to a witness who was not involved and who seems to have hardly any knowledge. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope that this will not be a part of my 15 minutes because the Prosecution is trying to interfere with the amount of time given to me. I'm going to put the question to the witness and then you'll see why I was giving the introduction I was giving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'm simply trying to ask the question with regard to the first map. Can you read what it says in item 4.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 4 it says under the jurisdiction of the Main Staff of the UN, and at the same time the centre of the new state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Ask you reply by looking at the map what it refers to, could you identify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it's the same objection under the same circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's unclear -- the witness is not here to interpret maps, Mr. Krajisnik; the witness is here to tell us about what he knows. So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can stop my questioning now, but I'm just trying to assist the Trial Chamber by indicating those maps. I think we need to establish whether these are the true maps, the authentic ones because the last time around the Prosecution submitted the wrong ones and I simply want to establish that Sarajevo was being suggested by the Serb side as a unified city. That's my aim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The proper way of doing that is calling your own witnesses who could support that, Mr. Krajisnik, and not by asking a witness who has hardly or no knowledge of this. You're not invited to stop your cross-examination; you're invited to continue your cross-examination in accordance with the Rules. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Tupajic whether he is aware of the fact that the Serb side -- or rather, what was the attitude on the part of the Serb side in the beginning with regard to Sarajevo and at the time of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what you said before, Mr. Krajisnik, it would follow that Sarajevo had been indicated as a city that should be under the jurisdiction of the UN, and I suppose that I think that the proposals from the Serb side went along those lines as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Document number 4, six strategic goals. I would like to ask a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, under 4 I have a heap of documents. Or did you change the order -- we received a couple of days the red --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not change it. The chapter is entitled "strategic goals" and I'm going to refer to that document now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A chapter from what exactly? It seems to be a book. What book is it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Owen's book, Balkan Odyssey. But my question is entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd like to know -- if you present me with a document I would like to know what it is. So it's the book from Dr. Owen. And now please put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you had deputies in the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Were you informed that the strategic goals had been adopted at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. Were you informed that they had been adopted or not or were you not informed at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat what I've said. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the minutes of the 16th session dated 12 May 1992. Could you please find it. It is in the bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under what tab, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minutes of the 12th -- under 4 one of the documents is the minutes of the 16th session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... pages 42 and 43?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 00847711 in the Serbian and this is the minutes and could you please look at item 1. You are looking at the transcript which had been appended to that document but it is a separate document. You're right in saying, Your Honour, what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I found it. It seems to be the last portion -- no the semi-last portion of the documents under tab 4. I've found it, Mr... We'll check whether it's in evidence and whether we have a translation already. 12 of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was in use during the period when Mr. Treanor was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have the minutes of the 16th session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you please read what it says here under item 1, the conclusions. On page 2, 00847712.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. An overview of the political situation of the territory in the Serbian territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was submitted by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the Council for National Security. After the discussion on this overview the deputies adopted information on the political and war situation. It was concluded that a working group should be established that would draw up a map of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina so as to find out what territories had to be defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And now can you go back, two pages back. This is a transcript of the session that took place on the 12th of May. Could you go back, please, back not forward but back in the minutes. 00487753.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the page can you read the conclusion under that item.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I would like to ask you. Could we please adopt this information. Your proposals and conclusions are welcome. Do we have to do it one by one? No, we don't have to. All right then. Who is in favour. Is there anybody against, anybody sustaining [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: All right then, you don't have to go on. I'm going to ask you to look at this item of the agenda and within this item in the same minutes the page number is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you asked the witness to read from what seems to be page 38 of minutes, last four ERN digits 7753. It is totally unclear whose words are reflected in these minutes. It seems that someone is speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the transcript. This was the proposal of the chairperson, Momcilo Krajisnik, about the first item of the agenda. We can look at the transcript, but I wanted to speed up. This is the item based on which the conclusion was passed after the discussion on the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever you draw our attention to minutes and whenever you want to draw our attention to something somebody said, at least it would be good to first identify on that transcript who is speaking. I can't see it on that page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I thank you. You are right, Your Honour. I wanted to have as little paper as possible and I wanted to finish as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it when you asked the witness to read this that you asked the witness to read what you considered to be your own words reflected in these minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I want to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you see here a proposal and the conclusion or the result of the voting after the information that I provided?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the text that I read, I see that the deputies voiced their opinion on the information that they had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's really of no use to ask someone to read minutes of a meeting, the Chamber could do it itself, unless the witness has any specific background information or if the witness is in a position to add something to that. But you just ask him to read and then you ask him: Does it say this and that. Of course the Chamber can do that as well. There are other ways of introducing such documents and there are other ways to draw the attention of the Chamber to these kind of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik acknowledged that this document is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course I do not know for sure. I can't search ERN numbers, but at least some of these documents are already in evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't have a specific recollection myself, but Mr. Krajisnik prefaced his remarks by admitting precisely that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik, and keep in mind that most important is that you can add questions that might not come up in the mind of Defence counsel because they were not there at relevant times and you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My question is as follows. Are you now why you were not informed that the strategic goals had been adopted or do you not remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember and I can't see it from the text that I have read out. I cannot conclude what the contents of the information were, the one that the deputies voted on, whether this information referred to the strategic goals or to something else. It is very difficult to see that clearly from such a short passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. If I now put it to you that during the submission of that information there was a discussion on the strategic objective, would your conclusion be different? Would you be able to pass any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then my conclusion would be that the information was adopted and that this information contained the strategic objectives that we are talking about in one form or another. That would be my conclusion after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well then. In 1992, did you receive the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well then. Were you informed that at the 16th session the Republika Srpska sent a request to the European Community to continue negotiations about the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such a request from that session, but I know that there were several initiatives on the part of the Serbian side at that time. However, I really don't know that anything was sent from that session to that effect. I only know that there were such initiatives.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the Chamber allow me to ask the witness to read a passage from the page 43 where Mr. Kuljevic [phoen] is speaking? I would like to remind the witness's memory and remind him of the request that was sent from that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to invite the witness to read the whole two-thirds, first part of page 43, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the whole request should be read out because it contains the positions that were put forth at that session and I believe it will be of great assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what would then your question be once you have invited the witness to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question will be as follows: Although Republika Srpska had declared its independence, did it ask for negotiations in order to seek a political solution, that it did not opt for the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You perhaps ask this question and let's see whether he has an answer to it. Mr. Krajisnik would like to know from you, Mr. Tupajic, whether, although Republika Srpska had declared its independence, whether it did ask for negotiations in order to seek a political solution and it did not opt for the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but I think that's two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the first is whether it asked for negotiations in order to seek a political solution. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you also aware that it did not at that moment opt for the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because -- let me repeat. Officially I was not informed about the existence of the strategic goals. As far as I can remember, nobody ever openly renounced those strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, any additional question in this respect? I think that there's -- unless there is a specific line in which you find such renouncement to the strategic goals, I think it makes not much sense to ask the witness to read page 43.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You have mentioned my visit and an objection that I put to you ever so mildly [Realtime transcript read in error: ever so"] about the Cyrillic script. Could you please tell the Chamber first what is the Cyrillic script. Who uses it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I have an objection. And I think it's a reasonably significant one for -- if Mr. Krajisnik is going to continue asking questions and that is he should not build into his questions testimony. I don't remember any language earlier about "ever so mildly" and Mr. Krajisnik is now attempting to testify about what was said on that occasion. I have no objection to the question in principle but I will object to any efforts by Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the last question. The question was as follows: "You have mentioned my visit and an objection that I put to you ever so about the Cyrillic script." I remember that the witness testified that Mr. Krajisnik insisted on the use of Cyrillic script and that the witness answered that they had better things to do, to say it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And it's -- I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now the question is: Could you please tell the Chamber: What is the Cyrillic script and who uses it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. And I have no objection to the question and as you can see there is a word that doesn't appear on this transcript and that was you have mentioned -- contained in the sentence you have mentioned my visit and an objection I put to you ever so mildly about he Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I missed that. Mr. Krajisnik, whether you were mild at that moment is not in evidence and you add that in your question. So you add information which is -- of course you could have asked the witness whether you were asking it with great insistence or mildly or not mildly. That's -- you can ask the witness but you cannot introduce that in a question. I missed that word, Mr. Tieger. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is an additional material that I was provided by the Prosecution. There is a statement by Mr. Tupajic there where he said that the objection was mild and he testified here that the objection was rather serious and I used the words from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may confront the witness with his statement if you want to do so and ask him questions about it. You cannot just let slip in the -- your own opinion on what happened in questioning the witness. Please put your question to the witness. Mr. Tupajic, Mr. Krajisnik would like to know what the Cyrillic script is. I think as a matter of fact the Chamber is aware of what the Cyrillic script is, unless any specific detail of it you would like to know. Mr. Krajisnik, we have seen now for one and a half years the Cyrillic script and it is not my first case in this Tribunal. So therefore the Chamber is aware of what the Cyrillic script is unless you would like to ask something very specific about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: According to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question you put is: Who uses it? Do you want an answer of the witness? The Chamber is aware that it's often used by the Serbian -- Okay. I do understand that you want to move to your next subject. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't want to talk about the Cyrillic script, I just wanted to lay the background, but I'm going to move on to another question that will explain my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: According to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, was the Cyrillic equal with the Latinic script?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Were there any machines using the Cyrillic before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The machines, the typewriters with the Cyrillic letters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. My first question -- my first answer was wrong. I apologise. I was not aware. When I joined the municipality of Sokolac, as far as I can remember, here we have the meetings of the sessions of the Crisis Staff, and I believe these minutes are in the Latinic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the years leading up to the war, in the years 1990 and 1991. Before the war were there in Bosnia and Herzegovina a single newspaper in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that for a fact, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Was there a company with an inscription or a logo in Cyrillic? Your company, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well, its name was in Latinic and I believe the majority companies were in Latinic. There may have been some in the Cyrillic script, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tupajic, you were the president of the municipality of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Was my objection mild or was it not, that is not important. However, was I authorised to remove the president of the municipality of Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Who was it who appointed the president of the municipality of Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputies of the municipality of Sokolac, according to the proposal of the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And who removed them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also the deputies of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, could that person either appoint or remove somebody, he personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm familiarised with the authorities of the institutions in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he couldn't do it directly. He could do it through the National Assembly that he presided over, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me now clarify. As a person, as a figure, could Momcilo Krajisnik either appoint or remove somebody? Would you be able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: About the oil chapter, if you remember the conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Bjelica where Krajisnik's name is mentioned, do you know in 1991 what position Momcilo Krajisnik occupied, in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first general election, multi-party election in Bosnia and Herzegovina you were appointed the president of the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik, you did --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness understands it to be what positions you held in the BiH and in Republika Srpska in 1991 and 1992. It's not in dispute. If I remember well, it's even among the agreed facts. I'm not quite sure about that, but if not then at least we have abundant evidence on the positions you are now asking for, unless you have any specific position in mind which is not clear in your question. Please proceed. I'll give you another five minutes. I'll be more flexible because -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, could you bear with me. I have just one more area to cover and I'll speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you have five minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, could the president of the Assembly have a company that he could use to trade in oil? First let's talk about Momcilo Krajisnik and then about Mirko Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I never --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik, could he have a company?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether the law was in place on the incompatibility of the two positions. Was there a law on the conflict of interests? I can't say that. As far as I know there was a company in the name of your brother, Mirko Krajisnik. He was in charge of that company as far as I know. However, I was not involved in that and it's very difficult for me to say this for a fact. I can only say that I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If I were to put it to you that there was a document that the Prosecution was supposed to give you -- but first let me ask you this. The document -- I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you refrain from comments on what the Prosecution should have done in respect of its own witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise. I apologise to the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber. If I do so something wrongly, it is probably down to my lack of experience and I hope that you will have patience with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The Prosecutor presented a document to the Trial Chamber that was published by Slobodna Bosna this is an agreement between the SDS and Rijeka Domisen Bosna [phoen]. The date is 21st of November, 1991 and the number is 02088340. You have it amongst your documents at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Krajisnik to repeat the ERN number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, under what tab are we seeking this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I believe that it would be easy to locate the document. I apologise. I have two copies. Could the Judges be provided with the document. This is Prosecutor's number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not insist on you tendering that document if it's not in evidence; it might be. But the witness seems to know what document you are talking about. Could you tell us what document your answer referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is not aware of this document but the Prosecutor has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you asked the witness: Have you ever seen this document before? The witness said: No, which means that he should have an idea on what document your question is about. Could you tell us, Mr. Tupajic, what document you had in mind when your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document entitled "3 dinars, Comrade Dukic." I have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you find that? Under tab number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of the binder that I have before me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is part of the documents that were provided by the Prosecutor yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now see what you have there. "3 dinars." You said you've never seen that document before. Next question, please, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you whether the Prosecution has shown you this document in order to shed light on things.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that my brother did not own a company at that particular point in time, and I've got the official document to prove that as well, could you maybe explain or interpret that conversation differently then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, on the basis of that conversation it follows quite clearly that someone in the Krajisnik family did own an oil company; there's no argument about that. As to what exactly it was, I did not know at the time and I don't know now. So I would not really venture into any clarification of relations and relationships that I knew nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the witness is drawing conclusions from something he heard, conclusions if to be drawn would be for the Chamber to draw. And it seems that he has hardly any additional knowledge. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know this will ever be significant, but the document to which Mr. Krajisnik is referring entitled "3 dinars for," is -- was not part of the materials to my knowledge that were part of yesterday's packet or part of the original presentation packet. I seem to recall that that was a document that was presented earlier in the case, but it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krajisnik, it's of no use to ask the witness, as he does draw inferences from conversations. Is there anything else you would like to ask the witness? I give you an opportunity to put a last question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- could I just ask two more questions, one in relation to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One. Mr. Krajisnik, I said one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You set up the autonomous Serb region Romanija and Birac. Do you remember that? You did say that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the two areas were set up separately, Romanija and Birac separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In that case we'll refer to Romanija only. What was the task with regard to the SAO Romanija, the independent, or rather the autonomous region of Romanija? Was it a part of your plan to chase away all the Muslims and have an ethnically cleansed territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not at the time. It was an initiative which had been embraced in order to indicate and submit to the public opinion in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the areas in which objectively speaking Serbs were in the majority and in terms of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina it would be taken into consideration. I believe that was the whole idea of setting up this autonomous area of Romanija that I'm familiar with and there were no special competencies with regard to the municipalities making up this region of Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did you function as such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I said you had one question. You claim two -- you had two, and you now ask for a third one. Your time for cross-examination is finished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Bench has no questions to the witness, Mr. Tieger, is there any need to -- for re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, any -- well, the questions by the Bench could not have triggered any need for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour, no. I have nothing further that I wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tupajic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- before I give you an opportunity to do so I promised you at an earlier stage that if you'd like to add anything and you had something on your mind which had to do with you being removed from your function by Mr. Ashdown, you have an opportunity now to add what you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to try and keep it as brief and concise as possible. I was a bit hurt by Mr. Stewart's performance yesterday when he tried to discredit me, not as a witness but first and foremost as a person. I would like to ask Mr. Stewart to submit to the Trial Chamber the document referring to my removal as a member of the Main Board and an MP in its entirety. It follows from the text of the document that I don't bear any personal, individual responsibility because there is not a shred of evidence to support that. And I'm aware of what role I played within the party. And as a president of the Deputies' Club of the SDS party in the Republic of Serbia before the last congress of the party - because the last one took place this year - we had a significant change of course, as it were, and we made a major contribution to the reforms in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And let me simply refer to the reforms of the customs system, the tax system, the defence, the judiciary, the security services, and the intelligence services. And secondly, as the head of that club, I actively participated in all that work appeared I assisted Mrs. Biljana Maric in drawing up the law on the cooperation with the Hague Tribunal and the MPs of the Serb Democratic Party that I tried to influence as much as possible. They passed it together with their colleagues of Muslim ethnicity. And the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence and I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a single sentence, Mr. President. And the fact that I'm in the same group -- put into the same bunch, as it were, as those who are banned from any further political activity was simply because I was president of that association of MPs and there was this link between the Presidency and the National Assembly. And basically nobody else, apart from another person, was in the National Assembly and we tried to make sure that we had better coordination. That was all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. It is not uncommon when a witness's credibility and reliability is tested in cross-examination that he experiences this as unpleasant. That's what happens, and thank you for your further explanation of the circumstances and -- under which you are banned from further political activity. I'd like to thank you from having come to The Hague -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I was just going to say the -- in response to the witness's request that the whole of that decision should go in, I would positively now wish to put the whole of that decision in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it that you'll tender that as a Defence exhibit now. You have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've got one marked copy, but we'll run off some copies as soon as we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you may have heard that Mr. Stewart follows your invitation and that he'll make available to the Trial Chamber the whole of the document he gave some quotes of. Again, thank you for the third time. I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, you may escort Mr. Tupajic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you'd like to tender into evidence any of the documents you used, we'd like to know within one week which ones exactly and we expect a translation to be provided. Translation of the maps not needed. But I wonder if it makes any sense to tender these maps with which you confronted the witness. Then, Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We are ready with one exception, Your Honour, and that is I would ask for an early break for two reasons. Number one, I think we would need some opportunity to set things up for the next witness. And number two, we're operating shorthanded because of a family emergency on the part of a critical member of our trial support team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could have an early break of approximately 30 minutes, that would be most helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take those 30 minutes also to -- no. We'll give you an early break. There's one issue -- let's deal already with the Prosecution exhibits; it's a long list. Mr. Registrar, could you give us the starting number and the last number of Prosecution exhibits in relation to this witness. If you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we changed registrars, we'll do it at a later stage. We'll have a break until 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is it you or Mr. Gaynor you takes the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next witness is Mark Thompson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could the witness be escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Usher. For Mr. Thompson we are in a 92 bis/94 bis hybrid situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. We have submitted his expert report a couple of years ago and we have submitted an addendum to that expert report more recently. We will be asking for those to be tendered -- we will be tendering those in evidence and we have selected from the report one document itself and from the addendum to the report a further seven documents which we will be tendering in order to fully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps for logistic reasons they might already have been distributed and they will be assigned numbers when it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I take it you are Mr. Thompson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thompson, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out by the usher. I now invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Thompson. I take it that Mr. Gaynor has explained the procedure, which is that a summary will be read from your written report and annexed to it and that you will then be cross-examined. I don't know whether you have any additional questions to the witness, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the choice for 92 bis assumes that it should be really limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be under 94 bis as well if you introduce the expert report. So then a few questions will be put to you by Mr. Gaynor. You'll then be cross-examined by the Defence. Mr. Gaynor, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Mark Thompson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You are of British nationality?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you explain any degrees which you hold?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I have a BA in English literature from the University of Cambridge and a PhD in social sciences from the University of Cambridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please tell us subject of your PhD.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It was on media and politics, with the focus on what I had written and published about the use and misuse of media in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you first visit Yugoslavia in 1987?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you travel in the former Yugoslavia in the late 1980s and early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you write a book based on those experiences entitled "A Paper House: The Ending of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you move to Zagreb in Croatia in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you speak and understand the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How long were you based in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I lived there from the summer of until the end of 1995, and then again from the autumn of 1996 until the -- April of 1999. There were some absences amounting to periods of months during those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While you were in Zagreb did you work for a period as a journalist, including a period working for the Guardian and the Spectator?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Not the Spectator. It was the New Statesman. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Are you an author of the book entitled "Forging War: The Media in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What briefly is that book about?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The book is about the pattern of political control of influential media outlets in those three countries and it is about the content of those influential media outlets and it is about the connection between the political control of outlets and the content of outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you describe how your book was received?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: When the book was published in the summer of 1994, it was very well received and reviewed in the United Kingdom and I remember also in the USA and Scandinavia. There were some criticisms -- the -- I don't remember any strong criticism -- or even any criticisms of the book, except those published in Croatia and Serbia by media outlets close to the governments in those countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where were you primarily located for the period during which you researched that book?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you travel elsewhere in order to research the book?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I went to Belgrade and to Sarajevo. That was in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And during what period approximately did you research the book?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Approximately the last four or five months of 1993 and I continued to gather information in the first four months of 1994 when I was mainly writing up the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the book itself is not before the Court. Could you explain for the Judges the sources which you consulted in the course of carrying out your research for that book.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I used as many sources as I could, including interviews with journalists who were involved in the media outlets that I wanted to investigate, involving analysts in those countries and also elsewhere in western Europe who were well informed about the media and the role of the media in the war. I used as many printed sources as I could. I used newspaper archives in Zagreb and in Belgrade for that purpose. And I employed journalists who were bilingual in Zagreb and Belgrade to help me do that research because it was an enormous amount of material to be surveyed. In Sarajevo the situation was of course much more difficult for research; the situation was chaotic. I tried to find archives of recordings of news programmes put out on the main television networks. I managed to do that partly in Zagreb, where I got limited access to the Croatian state television archive. I couldn't manage anything of the kind in Belgrade, though I tried and I did speak to people at the state broadcaster. In Bosnia it was, as I said, an extremely chaotic situation. I couldn't find any recorded archives at all. I did manage to find archives of newspapers, newsprint, which I used. And I should add that I interviewed journalists in all three places, Zagreb, Belgrade, and Sarajevo, but I've said that actually, haven't I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In preparing your expert report for this Tribunal, did you rely to an extent on the research which you carried out in your preparation for the book entitled Forging War?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you also rely on documents which was provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose now to read a summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Dr. Mark Thompson is the author of an expert report on the use of Bosnian Serb and Serbian media to disseminate messages to the Bosnian Serb people, the people of Serbia, and the international community in 1991 and 1992. He has previously authored a number of books, including Forging War, a study of the manipulation of public opinion by government-controlled media in Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In his report, Dr. Thompson concludes that the SDS in Bosnia successfully brought media outlets under its control and, using those media as megaphones, sought to convince Serbs that their very existence was threatened by Muslim and Croat genocidal tendencies, fuelled by ambitions for independence. He states that, far from performing the usual "watchdog" role of media in a democracy, the media outlets under actual or effective SDS control were used to block, express, and marginalise information and opinion that dissented from the SDS orthodoxy. There was wholesale support in this effort from influential media outlets in Serbia, in particular RTS, the Serbian state broadcast network. Dr. Thompson identifies the following eight areas which in his opinion demonstrate the SDS leadership's determination to control media outlets: 1, Attacks on, and efforts to divide Radio-Television Sarajevo RTVSA; 2, establishing control over RTVSA transmitters; 3, attacks on the premises and staff of Oslobodjenje newspaper; 4, establishing control of Glas newspaper, based in Banja Luka; 5, establishing control of the TVSA studio in Banja Luka; 6, establishing control over Radio Banja Luka; 7, establishment of SRNA (the news agency of the Bosnian Serb Republic), SRT (the radio and television corporation of the Bosnian Serb Republic), and printed media in Serb-controlled areas; 8, the issuance of instructions from SDS and Republika Srpska bodies to secure control of media entities. Dr. Thompson sets out the contents of the messages broadcast by media outlets under SDS control, which include warnings to the effect that: 1, the Serbs faced a threat to their very existence from Muslims and Croats; 2, the Serbs had to recall and learn from their previous experience of genocide in 1941-1945; 3, the Serbs' history of victimisation laid an obligation on the Serbs to mobilise in defence of the people; 4, the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina had to defend their right to live in a joint state with Serbs from Serbia and Croatia, and had to prevent the creation of a Muslim state in Europe, and the SDS was best equipped to help the Serbs succeed in achieving these objectives; 5, at this critical juncture, the Serbs were alone, betrayed by other peoples in the former Yugoslavia, and misunderstood and underestimated by the West; 6, the gravity of the threat facing the Serbs justified any measures that they might take an advance against their putative enemies. In an addendum to his report, Dr. Thompson refers to a number of statements by the accused which in Dr. Thompson's opinion conform to the patterns of media content described in his report. That ends the summary. Your Honours, I don't know how you wish Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to handle this, but I would like to tender the selection of the documents without putting them to the witness. Or that could be done at the end of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's better to do it now so they can be used in cross-examination if need be. Mr. Registrar, could you please, then, following the list provided by Mr. Gaynor, assign exhibit numbers to these documents, the first one being the report by Dr. Mark Thompson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will certainly do so, Your Honour. The first document will receive the provisional exhibit number P847. The second document, addendum to the report will receive P848. The third document, video of interviews of Krajisnik and Karadzic, will receive the reference P849. The fourth document, copy of interview with Momcilo Krajisnik, will receive the reference P850. The fifth document entitled video of interview with Krajisnik will receive the reference P851. The sixth document, a photocopy of Glas Srpski newspaper will receive the reference P852. The seventh document, the video of interviews with Krajisnik for death of Yugoslavia will receive the reference P853. The eighth document entitled video of interviews of Krajisnik on TV Banja Luka will receive the reference P854. The ninth document entitled Krajisnik addressing a crowd in Foca would receive the reference P855. And finally, the last document entitled the information system of Republika Srpska, article by Velibor Ostojic will receive the reference P856. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, did you do all the work and the examination of the materials for your report on your own, unaided by any assistant or team?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No. As I mentioned, I had the help of two -- as far as I remember, two people, one in Belgrade and the other in Zagreb and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they were -- what were they? Qualified researchers or what?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No. I told them what I was looking for. I was looking for articles from particular dates in particular newspapers, and they made notes. It was just to save time. I mean they -- to save my time. It wasn't a matter of them designing, as it were, the material that they were providing to me. I told them what I needed and went in the case of Zagreb and Belgrade to the newspaper archives with them and got them going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: And they provided notes to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So they were -- without any disrespect to them, they were basically gophers for the material and it was your work on the report?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I mean, they were -- in terms of their input to this report, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your report you say that your report has a limited scope, and this is on page 2, and does not purport to review the use of the media by all parties. Is it correct that in fact you didn't accept in so far as it might be incidental to your work, you didn't consider the use of the media by the other parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's consistent with the brief I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The brief from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say that before and during their armed conflict the principal political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina took the media very seriously. What are the dates that you put on the armed conflict for these purposes? You talked about before and during, so what's the period, the reference period there?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: You mean with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, the conflict started at the end of March 1992 and I suppose that you could date the beginning of the -- what people have called the media war in Bosnia to the seizure of transmitters, which is a matter that I've presented in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- actually you said -- you asked me a question, which on that occasion I answered, did I mean with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps I should put it a different way because it is your report, after all. So when you referred to "before and during their armed conflict the principal political parties took the media very seriously," I think I should ask you first, are you talking just about the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina or are you talking about the wider armed conflicts in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Oh, the regimes in all parts of the former Yugoslavia caught up in the war took media messages and media control extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what would you give -- adapting that question. You say "before and during their armed conflict." So that wider armed conflict, you would date it from when to when?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Oh, openly it would be from the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Until the autumn of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You go on in your report: "During the period in question," and then you define it as 1991 to 1992. Do we take it that the reason for your narrowing down the period in question to 1991 and 1992 is because you had been given the -- what I call the indictment period for Mr. Krajisnik's case as the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I'd been asked to focus on that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know what the period of Mr. Krajisnik's alleged crimes is in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No. I didn't discuss the indictment with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does the period 1st of July, 1991, to 31st December, 1992, does that closely match the period that you were asked to focus on for your report?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Not that I remember, no. There was reference to 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But that was what you were specifically asked to look at, 1991 and 1992, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say that the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party proved to be more resolute, more capable, and more successful than its rivals, and you identify them as the SDA and the HDZ, at bringing media outlets under its control. So it being relative, is the position that from what you've seen, all three parties did what they could to bring the media outlets under its control, it's just that in your view the SDS were more successful?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't think it would be true to say that all three parties did as much as they could, no. I think that there was an uncertainty, for example, in the SDA party as how to handle the question of media. I didn't -- I'm not aware of -- I haven't encountered any signs of such uncertainty in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what uncertainty and what way did the --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, for example, after -- during 1991 and early 1992, there was political pressure on the main republican media outlets based in Sarajevo to segregate their coverage ethnically and -- and even to institutionalise that kind of ethnic segregation. From what I was able to find out, the SDA was induced to desist from pursuing that path more easily than the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And induced by whom?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, by resistance for -- on the part of the media -- the journalists at those outlets, supported to some extent by Sarajevo civil society. There were -- there was at least one street demonstration in support of undivided -- ethnically undivided media in Sarajevo during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So was this -- was this the SDA succumbing to pressure or was it the SDA coming to the conclusion that it was in their interests not to keep pressing to hard?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible to answer that question, but the result is clear that the SDA did not pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't know of anything to suggest that the SDA would have desisted from attempts to control and use the media if they considered it was in their interest to do so, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Would you agree that the SDA would only have desisted from attempts to control or exploit the media if that's what they considered in their interests?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I can't say. I -- I'm not aware of any records or statements on that. I suspect that there was confusion at high levels in the SDA on this matter as on other matters; that there were different strands of opinion regarding media control. Certainly during the remainder of -- during the war they were -- and even after the war there were different strands of opinion, as it were, more or less hard line in the SDA on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the softer-line view in the SDA was what, that it was counterproductive for them to bring heavy pressure on the media?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The softer line within the SDA would be that it was not appropriate for the politicians to subject the republican media outlets to total political control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: As I said before, I don't know the reasoning which would have led the SDA to desist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You talk about using these media as megaphones. What -- isn't the media always going to be used as megaphones by political parties as much as they reasonably can?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, it's sensible to expect politicians to want influential media to convey their messages without counter-argument, but of course it's the job of media to provide arenas of discussion and debate and to provide information which will allow the public to reach informed decisions about matters of great importance to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether you're implying anything pejorative by your use of the word "megaphones" there.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
