utterances.text: I am implying something pejorative in that it is a abuse of media both by politicians when they happen to control media outlets and by journalists who submit to such control, when they allow media to, as I say, turned into loud-hailers for projecting, broadcasting political messages without debating those messages, without subjecting those messages to due examination and without putting them in the context of information about those messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say that the SDS sought to convince Serbs that -- and then you say "their very," and then you put in brackets "('biological') existence in Bosnia and Herzegovina was threatened by Muslim and Croat genocidal tendencies." Where do you get that the "biological" that you put in there very specifically in inverted commas? Where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It's a word that was used at the time and I would believe that it's somewhere in the material that I was given by the Tribunal -- sorry, in the material I was given to review when preparing this report. Those are the existential terms that were bandied around at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We see an example of that, don't we. It's the text of footnote 39, it's on the foot of page 11 of your report. It starts at the foot of page 11. So last sentence: "While defining both outlets as 'non-party and independently orientated,' this statement," which is from a local newspaper, "said, they 'must affirm the truth about the position of the Serb people, inform Bosnia and Herzegovina about its relationship with other peoples and the permanent genocide against the Serb people in the 20th century as also about the war that was imposed on the Serb people at the moment it rose up in defence of its biological and national survival in its own land." So it's that type of source from which you draw the word "biological"?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: That's one, but as I say, this was a word which was in the ether a great deal at that time in these kind of contexts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in a nutshell it all harks back to an undoubted genocide against the Serbs in Croatia in the Second World War, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Can you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It -- in a nutshell it harks back to an undoubted genocide against the Serbs in Croatia during the Second World War, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: These messages did, yes, constantly go back to the fate of the Serbs in Croatia and also -- well, and at that time also Croatia during the Second World War included Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and you say the SDS sought to convince Serbs that their biological existence was threatened and so on by the Muslim and Croat genocidal tendencies fuelled by ambitions for independence. It was very clear, at least by early 1992, that the Muslim nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina or many of its leaders harboured ambitions for independence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That's beyond question. But the big lie of the SDS propaganda was the alleged genocidal tendencies. The claim, in other words, that for the Muslims and the Croats, the road to independence was one which would lead the Serbs to perdition, extermination indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There were at least, whether or not in your view, Mr. Thompson, justified, there were genuine fears among the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't there, about perspective [sic] independence of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed there were. And the fears were genuine. The issue, though, is what was the source of those fears. Why were those fears. That is the issue which I have addressed in my report. I wouldn't at all contest that they were genuine fears, widespread among the Serbs of Bosnia, as they were of the Serbs of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you're not saying those fears were entirely stirred up by the SDS, are you?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I would say that I don't believe, and nothing I've read has led me to believe, that there was an existential threat to the Serbs of Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you, Mr. Thompson. Put on one side for the moment that, in your view, extreme position. The fears among Serbs about perspective independence of Bosnia, those were there and genuine without any stirring up by the SDS, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No. I couldn't agree that they -- I would say that it would be impossible to determine whether -- that those fears existed independently of the SDS. But I certainly would agree that the SDS did not solely invent those fears. Those fears were also being encouraged by the political leadership and opinion makers and cultural authorities in Serbia proper. And those messages from Serbia were of course relayed to the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just ask one question in between. We are talking about fears, we are talking about existential fears. This Chamber has heard quite some evidence on fear that would exist, fear being -- fear being that these Serbs when Bosnia and Herzegovina would become independent, that the Serb would a minority in such an independent state, whereas when Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain in a larger Yugoslavian context that they would feel that they are not just on their own as Bosnia and Herzegovina Serbs, Bosnian Serbs. But I'd like you when you answer any of these questions about fears to clearly distinguish between these kind of fears, the fear to become a minority, a national minority, ethnical minority, political minority, and existential fears, that is fear, as you said, to be exterminated. May I invite you to make that distinction whenever it's relevant to do so in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or don't you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an invitation but if you think that it needs some clarification, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can try to make the distinction you request, but I also want to point out that the blurring of that distinction was one of the main intentions and achievements of SDS propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the period in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if Mr. Stewart asks you -- let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is Your Honour thinking of page 48, line 13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, my first concern was to get a clear -- to get my mouse in the right spot. Yes. It was in that context when Mr. Stewart asked you: "Well, you're not saying that those fears were entirely stirred up by the SDS, are you?" Then I'd like to -- what he's -- where you said: "They were certainly not inventing it." If it would be possible for you to see what was perhaps invented and what was not invented or whether -- well, I'd like to have answers as precise as possible also in respect of the matter I just raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your footnote 2 to your report, you say -- well, the text of that footnote was that: "Far from performing normal watchdog role of media in a democracy, the media outlets under actual or effective SDS control were used to block, express, and marginalise information and opinion that dissented from the SDS orthodoxy." The first point is this, Mr. Thompson, would you agree to describe former Yugoslavia as a fully functioning democracy would not have been accurate throughout the 1980s right up towards the end of that decade.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I agree, it wouldn't be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that by 1991 it was Serbia particularly and the Yugoslavia of which it was a part was in a transitional change where it has not achieved full democracy, whatever that exactly might be.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I'm saying here that the former Yugoslavia was a full democracy. I was making an explanatory point to -- in order to try to clarify the nature of what was happening with the media outlets under SDS control. And as far as the watchdog role goes, there was, for example, a degree of pluralism in the Croatian media during the 1991 war and in the Sarajevo media during the Bosnian war that was considerably greater than that achieved by media outlets in areas under SDS control. So there was a kind of -- not perfectly performed, but there was a kind of watchdog role attempted by the media elsewhere during that time. So -- and this indicates that it should be been possible also in the areas controlled by the SDS, but it wasn't exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Croatia was a country, for want of a better word, Croatia was a country dominated by Croats at the beginning of 1991 forming part of a state whose capital was in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't see the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's agree that, Mr. Thompson, the -- so that pluralism of the media of the media in Croatia was more likely to be achieved, wasn't it, during 1991 in Croatia than in some other parts of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't understand your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if you don't agree with the proposition, then you don't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that there is an argument there, actually. There was a republican media space in Croatia. There was a republican space in Bosnia and Herzegovina which was carved up even before the start of open war in Bosnia. What I -- the point I was making is that even during the war within the republican territory of Croatia there was a degree of media pluralism which contrasts with that in the SDS-controlled -- Bosnian Serb-controlled portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a comparative point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say in the -- I read the passage to which footnote 2 is the footnote and you say, for example: "These outlets," though you're talking about the ones under actual or effective SDS control, "permitted no serious examination of the contradiction within the statements of SDS leaders in 1991 and early 1992," and the contradiction that you highlight is that on the one hand the Muslims were known to be the weakness of Bosnia's peoples and shouldn't dare to confront the Serbs, and on the other hand that it was the Serbs that faced the biological threat to their existence. Mr. Thompson, that contradiction in time of conflict where on the one hand at times you present yourselves as stronger in order to intimidate the enemy but on the other hand you might warn your own people that they were threatened is not a -- is not a unique or unexpected contradiction, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, for most of this period, 1991 and 1990 -- well, you see that I refer to 1991 and early 1992. There was no open conflict at that time. The -- what I had in mind when I wrote that specifically was the warning that Karadzic gave in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina I think in mid-October 1991 about the Muslims inviting their own destruction. I think the context was the debate on adopting a statute of sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't be --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: If I can just finish. So that was a clear threat against one of the three peoples of the republic and yet at the same time the SDS leaders and the media under their control or influence were saying that it was the Serbs who faced the very real and sort of present danger of being wiped out, and that -- that allegation, which is the gravest conceivable allegation, was not subjected to journalistic investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in a time of prospective conflict to threaten, well, I use the word the enemy, to threaten the enemy in such a way in such a way as to deter them from conflict while at the same time giving perhaps exaggerated warnings to your own people is not a unique or unusual or illogical thing it to do, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't accept your characterisation of the context there. And these were not exaggerated warnings. These were invented threats of the gravest possible kind. The warning was going out constantly to the Bosnian Serbs that they faced extinction, that there -- that there was a genocide hanging over their heads and that therefore, of course, if that -- if -- in that situation any means of self-defense become justified. Now, it's the job -- of course it's the job of politicians not to make such incendiary, misleading statements, but it's the job of professional media outlets to subject such grave political statements to examination. It's the elementary task of the fourth estate, and the point I was making there is that this was not attempted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who's the culprit then? Your journalistic colleagues for not doing their job?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The culprits are both the politicians and of course the staff at the media outlets concerned. They are -- I say the politicians because the politicians controlled the outlets. These are not media outlets in the western European sense. They were, as I said, they were megaphones. These were political tools which were being used politically to disseminate certain messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In Serbia at this time everyone was starting from a base of heavy control of the media anyway, wasn't one? Weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, that was the situation in Serbia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Thompson, I think it's implicit in your report, but you would agree, would you, that of all the media the one with overwhelming disproportionate impact dwarfing all other forms of media is television?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Broadcasting, certainly; I believe television, but some local analysts that I spoke to at the time believed that radio was extremely important. However, the impact of radio was impossible to judge because there weren't conditions where surveys could be carried out on listenership rates and so forth. So I believe that you're right but I would prefer to say broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's clear that then. If we lump broadcasting, television and radio together, then the proposition is great, it absolutely dwarfs all printed material in terms of its impact on the population, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To the point where not totally insignificant, but the significance of printed publications is really quite tiny in relation to the impact of radio and television combined.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It's certainly much less. Whether it's tiny, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- where you say "the outlets permitted no serious examination of that contradiction," do you suggest that television in the first place was likely at any point to engage in a serious examination of that contradiction?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It's certainly possible for television as a medium to conduct debates on political matters; it's -- it happens all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, how likely was it that television in this region at that time would have engaged in a serious examination of such a contradiction?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, the current affairs formats were used in -- by television networks at that time. Studio interviews and so forth were used. Journalists knew how to do that. And the -- there were phone-in programmes as well. So I don't see any reason to think that the television would be incapable of addressing that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with this broad division of the target for media or the people who were reached by media, four categories: The public in Serbia, I'm talking about 1991 and 1992. First, the public in Serbia; secondly, the Bosnian Serb public; thirdly, Bosnian Muslims and Croats, I'll put them together for these purposes; and fourthly, the international media and international community. Is that a sensible division?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I'm -- I think the answer may depend on which media outlets you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's talk about television, then, in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Television, the -- well, Serbian state television was of course primarily addressed to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia, but as I describe in my report, it was enabled to reach a very large and larger and larger proportion of Bosnia and Herzegovina through the seizure of transmitter infrastructure that longed to the Bosnia-Herzegovina state broadcaster. Now, as for the Bosnia-Herzegovina state broadcaster RTSA, that did not in its coverage during -- until, until spring of 1992, it did not attempt to address ethnic publics. Quite the opposite. It tried very hard to address a public that -- beyond ethnic segregation, beyond ethnic definition. So of course it found this very hard to do during -- for example, when it was covering the war in Croatia. But it did its best. And the same would be true of the republican flagship newspaper Oslobodjenje, but I'll stick to television for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll bring in print. Let's look at those four categories. The international media and community, would it be more receptive, do you agree, to the printed word as well as television?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, during 1991 and early 1992, there wasn't that much international coverage from Bosnia. All eyes were on Croatia until the Vance plan was signed. So that's my -- that's my recollection. So I don't think there was much in international coverage. And later on when there was -- when Bosnia was inundated with international journalists, they were mostly print because it -- and that's partly for technical reasons. At that time the technology to provide real time images by an isolated journalist or a small team in the field wasn't developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that -- working back up that list then, that's the international community. So far as -- I'll put Muslims and Croats together for these purposes. But, Mr. Thompson, we know that overwhelming as a proportion we're talking about Muslims in Bosnia rather than Croats for these purposes. We agree about that?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't know what you're going to say, so I don't agree with that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In contradistinction to Serbs. If we're talking about Serb exploitation of the media, I want to avoid having to ask too lots of questions, one in particular to Croats, one in particular to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It depends what outlets we're talking about. As I said, the Bosnia Herzegovina state government tried -- bent over backwards not to try and address one national public, one ethnic public rather than another. I have analysed this in my book. I don't think it enters much into the report at all. But that is what RTSA tried to do and indeed in the spring and summer of 1992 it caused frustration to some citizens in Sarajevo because it remained so ethnically vague in its -- in its language, in its coverage of what was happening in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: That's why I -- and I keep saying this because I don't accept the -- I don't want the implication to be accepted that somehow the Bosnia-Herzegovina state network was addressing an ethnic public. It wasn't. It was trying to address the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: SDS-controlled media would have had fairly little impact and cut no ice with the Muslim and Croat nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: SDS outlets?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The SDS-controlled outlets, as you described them in your report, they'd have had little impact on Muslims and Croats in Bosnia during the conflict. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, as sources of information, I would think so. But they were certainly -- for example, in Sarajevo there was a certain horrified fascination with the news bulletins of Bosnian Serb broadcasters, and these could be picked up in parts of Sarajevo and they were watched. So it wouldn't be true to say, in my experience, that there was a boycott by non-Serbs of Serb-controlled outlets, but it would be true to say that those outlets didn't enjoy credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've really answered the follow-up question. You talk in your report, and this is page 4, how the victorious -- after the 1990 elections "the victorious SDS-SDA-HDZ coalition drafted a new broadcasting law that would have led to the network splitting" up "into three national services." So it's clear that at that time all three of those parties wanted something which they were prevented from getting because that proposal was rejected by the federal constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The SDA then, as you describe it, abandoned its support for splitting up the network and then you say: "The SDS, by contrast, called out right in November 1991 for TVSA to be split into national channels." So the SDS were -- well, they were pressing for something which all three parties had previously wanted. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The SDA had by that time abandoned that policy, presumably because they considered it was pointless or not in their interests.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I think we've been over this ground before. I've got nothing new to add. I don't know. The SDA was confused on many strategic questions and this well -- the question of the key republican media outlets may well have been one of those questions, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You talk in general as your introduction to section B of the SDS leadership's determination to control media outlets and then you set out various actions in 1991 and 1992. It's not -- leave aside from the moment what you said about the actual message that was conveyed, a determination in circumstances of at least serious prospect of conflict to control media outlets is not inherently a surprising policy to adopt, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The way you put that rather blurs over that the threat of conflict was emanating from the party that was taking over the media outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, that -- is that an assumption or a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, it follows from the history of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The -- for example, the capture of RTVSA transmitters between August 1991 and March 1992 and continuing after March 1992, which I explain in pages 5 and 6 of my report, was carried out in order that the Serbian broadcaster -- basically so that Serbian broadcasting would be received as many Bosnian Serbs as possible and as many Bosnian Serbs as possible would not be able to see the output of TV Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll come to that specific matter. But Mr. Thompson, you said that my question had blurred over the fact that the threat of conflict was emanating from the party that was taking over the media outlets.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we can leave aside media outlets for the moment. The threat of conflict was emanating from the SDS or Bosnian Serbs. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Karadzic in the Assembly in October 1991, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you say, do you, that there was no implicit threat of conflict in any of the actions or pronouncements of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the threat of conflict being wielded by Bosnian Muslim political figures at that time. There was an awareness of the risk of conflict, absolutely, and that was reflected in statements given. But I don't recall that there was the threat made, namely, we can start a war against you if we want, and if we do you don't -- and if we do, you face extermination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The war in Croatia was precipitated, wasn't it, by Croats' declaration of independence?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't see the relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the answer is yes, is it, Mr. Thompson? Don't worry too much about the relevance for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I do, because I'm not here to discuss the outbreak of war in Croatia and the way in which -- the way in which political events led to the outbreak of conflict in Croatia is a complicated one and I don't want to digress into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Thompson, ultimately we're all under the direction of the Trial Chamber. But please -- actually, it is, with respect, your function to answer the questions and not to explore their relevance. The -- Mr. Thompson, the declaration of independence by the Croats was either the or a major precipitating cause of the conflict in -- of the war in Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the witness did not only say that he didn't see the relevance of your question; he also said that he is not here to discuss the outbreak of the war in Croatia and the way in which -- the way in which political events led to the outbreak of war in Croatia. He says "it's a complicated one and I don't want to digress into that." Is it that you do not want that because you feel that your expertise would not allow you to give answers to those questions or is there any other reason such as since it's complex it would take too much time or since it's complex you would further need to consult your sources? I just want to know why you didn't want to enter into that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for the question. It's a long time since I thought about that. I used to know -- I used to follow these events very closely, but I haven't thought about the outbreak of war in Croatia for years and if instructed to do so, I shall now do my best. I am not particularly comfortable doing so, but I will do so if required to do so. I still, by the way, don't see the relevance of the matter to the discussion in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, you should clearly draw yourself the lines where you are able and where you are confident that you can answer questions and where you're not. And please address me if you feel uncomfortable. Mr. Stewart, there's not a clear no from the witness. He explains why he has difficulties in answering your questions. It's not only a matter whether he sees the relevance of it, because that, I would agree with you, would be rather in the hands of Chamber. So you may put questions to him. But you, Mr. Thompson, you are instructed to immediately address if you are not confident that you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect I entirely accept the distinction you draw for the purposes of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, that -- as far as Bosnia was concerned it was -- it was clear, wasn't it, that a persistence by the Bosnian Muslims in pushing towards independence was very likely to precipitate conflict? I'm talking about violent conflict in that country.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It's clear that it was -- that it had the potential to do that. I'm not sure whether using the words "very likely" isn't being wise after the event. But of course it wasn't clear at the time that it could lead to conflict and the leaders on all sides acknowledged that, they referred to that, in their different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Going on to what you just mentioned about the capture of those transmitters referred to at page 5 of your report, you talk about five transmitters belonging to RTVSA being captured by Serb or Yugoslav army forces. Can I ask, you draw a distinction to Serb or Yugoslav army forces. So when you talk about Serb forces as opposed to JNA forces, do you mean the paramilitary forces that you mentioned a few lines further down? This is page 5, middle of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the Kozara transmitter captured you say by -- on the 1st of August, 1991, was that captured by Serb forces, as you just defined them, or by Yugoslavia or Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The Kozara transmitter, according to Javnost, a Bosnian -- an SDS course was captured by a paramilitary unit linked to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Captured from whom?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: From the owners and the owners were the RTVSA. The infrastructure -- the broadcasting infrastructure I believe belonged to RTVSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the links to the SDS, does your source, as you've just described it, say any more about those links?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I assume not. But it's an SDS source saying there were SDS links and there were, according to -- that's in 1993, that source. According to Oslobodjenje in March 1992, so trying to report it at the time, they were territorials and militia and also mentions the local SDS branch in Doboj being involved in a different theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where is Javnost based or where was it based in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't know. Pale probably. Banja Luka, Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and the Pljesevica transmitter, who was that captured from?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: The same answer. The transmitter network belonged to the republican broadcaster, belonged to RTVSA, but RTVSA had no forces on the ground to defend its infrastructure. So it seems extremely unlikely that there was shots exchanged at the transmitter sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- you referred to that transmitter the -- as being seized by Serb militia. Do you know more about who that --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll complete the question -- about who those Serb militia were. So your answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the Ciganiste in Doboj. You say the local SDS branch in Doboj organised the seizure of Ciganiste. Is that as much as you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so far as Majevica is concerned, what can you say about -- what do you know about who seized that from whom?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, that transmitter, like the others, ended up in SDS control, Bosnian Serb control, meaning SDS control, being used to -- for the same purposes as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that as much as you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so far as how you pronounce Trovrh?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Trovrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Trovrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Trovrh and Gorazde. You say at the foot of page 5: "The Serbs had occupied the transmitter in that place the previous day in response to the (alleged occupation by Muslim forces of a factory in Gorazde." By use of alleged are you saying you don't know there was such an occupation by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Correct. I'm not aware what organised Muslim forces there were in Gorazde in March 1992 or what the occupation of a factory would mean. And I was -- I was implying that the shape of this story has a propaganda shape, namely: We were carrying out this action in response to. The intention here is to justify the action taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your footnote 17 you refer to the text to that is you're talking about attacks on Oslobodjenje. In the second paragraph there you say: "The main threat was presented by the SDS, which considered the newspaper to be - like RTVSA - anti-Serb." Then you say: "In the months before open conflict started, kiosks owned by Oslobodjenje were vandalised. After open conflict started, the Serb-JNA forces were quick to target the newspaper. The Sarajevo offices were shelled systemically, regional correspondents were killed." Then in 17 footnote: "The Zvornik correspondent... Mr. Smailovic was murdered on the 8th the April on the doorstep of his office by Serb forces. He had observed these forces approaching as he filed his last piece." You get that from a newspaper report, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't remember any longer. It's more than ten years since I did that research. But of course it's a matter of record; this detail can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter of record that it's reported in that way.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Indeed. But the deaths would also be a matter of record. Those correspondents either died or they didn't, and -- I believe that the information there is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you have absolutely no knowledge now of -- when it says: "On the doorstep of his office by Serb forces," what those forces were?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't remember where that information comes from, but I clearly regarded it at the time as reliable and fit to be used, I mean in the first edition of my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You talk about control of Glas newspaper on page 7 and you say, third line: "After the 1990 elections the paper passed into the ownership of the municipality," so that was a legal process, was it, by which that happened?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I would assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you point out there that a municipality was controlled by the SDS, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- under section 6 on page 8 "control of Radio Banja Luka," second sentence or second line you say: "Late September 1991 with war waging in neighbouring Croatia, General Nikola Uzelac, commander the local JNA garrison, was given the hospitality of Radio Banja Luka to issue a general mobilisation to fight in Croatia." Now, first of all, Mr. Thompson, you know, do you, or would accept that the general mobilisation was an entirely legal matter? Lawful is what I'm meaning to say, that was a mobilisation issued in accordance with the law to which people were legally obliged to respond.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No, I don't express a view on the legality or illegality of the garrison commander's action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you don't know whether the mobilisation and to what extent the mobilisation was simply in accordance with the law of Yugoslavia, as it was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: My point here was to draw attention to the way in which the radio station was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it objectionable for a radio station to allow a senior officer to issue a mobilisation call if it is entirely in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I would call it an abuse, yes, of a local radio station to -- for it to be used to issue a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If a mobilisation call is entirely lawful, is it not entirely legitimate then for the authorities to use whatever media resources are at their disposal to disseminate that call among the population?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Information about a mobilisation may of course be given over a media outlet. But for mobilisation to be issued over the airwaves is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What's the distinction between information about a mobilisation and mobilisation to be issued?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, it's a rather important distinction. On the one hand, a media outlet is doing the professional job of a media outlet and reporting on significant current events; and on the other hand, the media outlet is being used as a megaphone of local military, in this case, or political, I would think both in this instance, authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, where you use the word "megaphone" here, do you just want to say that it's used as a means of communication for those who issue the -- who issue the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. It's being used as a public -- as a -- as a system of -- it's being used as a possession of the military, and it's not a possession of the military. And the radio station should not lend itself to being perceived by the public as a possession of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, I had some difficulties in understanding why the distinction the witness made, that is the distinction between information about the mobilisation and mobilisation to be issued over the airwaves, that that distinction was not clear. It was perfectly clear to me, but of course you're fully entitled to seek clarification if you do not understand it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I will proceed, with respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So information about a mobilisation which you regard as legitimate is when a media outlet says: One of today's stories is that a mobilisation call has been issued from such-and-such headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, followed by maybe quotation of the mobilisation notice, followed by perhaps an interview comment with the military or with political leaders from different -- different places on the political spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that's legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. It's more than --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Clearly in your view?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's normal reporting?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mobilisation issues, when as happened here, according to your report, the actual call is made by the military through the media.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's military, Mr. Thompson, but do you accept that if it is a legal mobilisation call, it is actually a significant and lawful act by the lawful authorities of that state?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I've already said what I think about the use of media in this way and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't answer my question, Mr. Thompson.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, the legality or the illegality of this was, of course, contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Thompson --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the collective Presidency of the republic and then defended by the -- by an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Our objection, Your Honour is this: that the witness has been asked about this issue and he's answered it and there's no new questions being asked by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, he hasn't quite and I am entitled to press this a little further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, it depends on the answers, Your Honour. If I get one or two answers to my questions, then it probably would be one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, I put a -- I put a question to you on a premise, which you then argued with. The premise was that it was a legal mobilisation call, a significant and lawful act by lawful authorities. That was the premise.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't accept the premise. If you look at footnote 23 it will be clear that the question of the legality of this action was clearly a very -- a very significant question at the highest levels of political authority in the country. And therefore, for the radio station to have allowed this use to be made of it in such a delicate and significant way is indicative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you understand what the -- what the difference was in relation to the legality or illegality of this mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I've said that clearly the question of the legality or illegality was a very pertinent and debatable matter, otherwise you would not have had the JNA garrison commander in the north of the country doing one thing and his action then being denounced as illegal by a collective -- by a body no less than the collective Presidency in the capital of the country. I've also said that even if the -- I've even -- I've also said that the question of legality and illegality does not entirely dispose of the question as to whether a radio station should allow itself to be used in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, do you understand the distinction is that the collective Presidency in Sarajevo were denouncing the mobilisation call as illegal in a way which implicitly rejected the view that the mobilisation call was based on the continuing integrity of the state of Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I've got nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you understand that was the question? Do you understand that distinction?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I would suppose that the grounds for deciding on the legality or illegality of the garrison commander's action would themselves be contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just try to -- we are moving away from where we started. Mr. Thompson, questions were put to you whether it was objectionable for the radio station to allow -- to issue a mobilisation call. You said you would call it an abuse. And slowly from objectionable and abuse we entered into the realm of legality or not. If you said it was an abuse, did you consider it to be an abuse in strictly legal terms or did you consider it an abuse in terms of what you expect the media to perform as a function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the latter, clearly; with regard to the former, I didn't express a view. This, of course, is in the context of presenting, of explaining, how it was that the different ways that the SDS used media outlets under its control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This radio -- if I may add one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This radio outlet would certainly have known that the question of issuing a mobilisation was -- that its legality would be open to question at the highest levels in the country. They would know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And therefore -- well, that has to be factored in when considering how to assess their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you did not give any specific opinion on whether in strictly legal terms a government or any military commander would be entitled under the existing law to use the media for this purpose, apart from whether you'd like it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't give an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if a media outlet is faced with a question as to the legality of something --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like just to clarify the position. This witness is being presented by the Prosecution as an expert on propaganda. Now, the legality at the republic and federal level of the mobilisation call is not an issue, in our submission, on which he can offer expert assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- I think I addressed that matter clearly. And of course if the witness would have said, no, I take a very clear position on the legality of that, we might have further explored what his expertise could be that he could make such a statement. But Mr. Stewart only said: "So if a media outlet is faced with the question as to the legality of something," he might want to ask the witness who pays for the advice or whatever. We do not know yet what the question of Mr. Stewart would be, and we'll first give him the opportunity to put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If the media outlet is faced with a question as to the legality of some step, action, then its first responsibility is to try to form a view as to the legality or not, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would have to do that. I mean, it should do that. Whether it would is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it should, all right. So if there is a contested view that the media outlet reaches a decision as to which of those contested views is correct, that's an entirely legitimate step for media outlet to take, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, so much of this is context-dependent. The media outlet should -- the decisions it makes in its internal deliberations is one thing. The way it reports a move which in itself is contested or inevitably going to be contested as soon as it is taken is another matter. And in order to shed more light on this we would need to have more information about the events of those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, your whole complaint was that this wasn't a report. So where your answer says "the way it reports is in itself contested" and so on. The question is this, Mr. Thompson: First of all -- and you didn't quite answer the question. If a media outlet is faced with a decision as to what action to take and that decision depends upon a view of the law, then its first responsible step is to try to reach a decision as to the legal position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: By all means internally and as a media outlet its duty is to report the issue to the public, to report that there is a debate, to report that there are different points of view on the matter in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the reporting side, Mr. Thompson.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But if it's in this case the media outlet was clearly being asked to take an action, that is to allow its facilities to be used to announce publicly the mobilisation. Right?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And step number one would be for them to form a judgement as to whether that mobilisation call was in accordance with or would be in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: That should be, yes. And also for whether it's appropriate for the station to lend itself to that use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's a second -- that's the next question I want to come to there, Mr. Thompson. If -- and please accept this for the purposes of this question as the premise. If the media outlet has come to the judgement that the mobilisation call is in accordance with the law --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. In those circumstances, do you still say that it is objectionable for that media outlet to be used simply for the announcement of that legal mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: You want a crystalline answer and I cannot give you one. This would depend upon the way the media outlet decided to report around the issue in question, in this case the mobilisation. It would depend on editorial decisions about how -- about which kinds of opinions they would give on the matter of the mobilisation. It would -- so that needs all to be taken into account. Now, should media outlets be used -- should public media outlets be used simply for the announcement of that legal mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what's your answer to that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: You mean should the garrison commander be allowed to sit in the studio and announce to the people that there is a mobilisation on the assumption, on the assumption then that the staff of the radio station are fully convinced of the full legality of that mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take that as the assumption. What's the answer?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Then they could. However, in this case, as I've said already, it would be clear to all concerned that the legality would be contested at very high and serious levels. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: So the staff at Radio Banja Luka were not in that position --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Because the legality was open to -- was contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, I've deliberately refrained from asking you any opinion as to the law, and I'm going to continue to do that. But do you agree that it is perfectly possible for a -- the staff of any media outlet, A, to recognise that there is a contested view as to the legal position but, B, to come to a firm conclusion as to which is the correct view?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if they have come to a firm conclusion as to which is the correct view, then it is their responsibility as journalists to follow that view, regardless of the fact that somebody else holds another view?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It's their responsibility to act as professional journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, why should they act son somebody else's view, Mr. Thompson, if they have formed a clear view themselves as to the legal position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene. There seems to be huge confusion, and I come back to what I said earlier, that is what I asked earlier about journalistic professionalism and legal matters. Having listened to both questions and answers for quite some time, I got the impression - but please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Thompson - that you would say that if it would be uncontested that there was a legal obligation to broadcast a mobilisation call - uncontested in legal terms - then you would say that law or that legal context in which you had to do that may have existed, but the duty of a journalist goes beyond that if they were in a position where they had, in order not to break the law, to broadcast such a call. Then, even if they did it and they had to do it, it was nevertheless the journalist's professional duty to report on circumstances of the mobilisation call, they should start a debate on whether such a law was right or not. So more or less they would, even if not in strict terms, they would be in a position of civilian inobedience even if they would acknowledge that they were under a duty under the existing law to publish this mobilisation call. Is that a correct understanding? Because we are again and again, I think, thinking on different levels. Is this more or less what you had in mind and which I tried to distil from I wouldn't say conversation but answers -- questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it is. I can quite imagine that under, for example, state of emergency legislation it would be obligatory upon media outlets to carry certain types of information, of course. Now, that doesn't absolve even in such a situation where the state of emergency would be undisputed and its legality undisputed, journalists still have a journalistic job to do, reporting to the public the discussion around the information which it is obliged to carry. This happens in -- this is not unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However, it's -- I don't know if -- I mean, I feel I should repeat that the response of the republican -- of the collective Presidency clearly indicates that there was no -- was no crystalline consensus on the legality of the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's a very specific matter for this mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I hope that my question added to avoid further confusion. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you say that a media outlet can only act on a view of the law as to which there's a crystalline consensus?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No, I don't say that and I'm not aware of having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, do you agree that there are two distinct issues here? This is one whether the media outlet should have been used to announce the mobilisation -- for the mobilisation call itself, and there is, secondly, the question of whether or not as a responsible media outlet it should have reported the fact that there was a dispute about the legal position.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't feel I've anything to add to our discussion of two sentences in my 20-page report. I don't think I can enlighten the Court any further on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, do you, in fact, have a view as to the legality of that mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: My view is that it was clearly contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock. I'd first ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Thompson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber considers the matter to be sufficiently dealt with at this moment of the legality and duties and professionalism -- professional duties of journalists on this subject. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. My next question would be how much time you would more need. It's not a trick, for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would expect to finish with a reasonable margin within the time left today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you think, as matters stand now, that you would have any additional questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will only have a couple of questions, three or four at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three or four. Would then, looking at how the witness answers questions, would -- well, let's say anything between five and ten minutes be enough?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, you're invited to see whether it would be possible for you to finish, well, approximately half past 1.00. We'll adjourn. We'll resume at 13 minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, on page 9 of your report you've got a section 8, "Instructions regarding media and information," you say: "As early as October 1991, when open conflict was still half a year away, the SDS leadership instructed Serb mayors," and so on. Mr. Thompson, how is anybody to know in October of 1991 that open conflict was still half a year away?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: They weren't to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know what had happened in mid-October 1991 to increase the prospect of open conflict? Well, do you know about a walk-out from the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly in mid-October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you agree that that clearly increased the prospect of open conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Can I inquire as to the relevance of this line of inquiry or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Mr. Thompson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, please. I think you refer to it even in a more indirect way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we -- this episode came up earlier. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The next paragraph of your report you talk about SDS -- what you describe as SDS main committees instructions for the organisation of activities and so on. May we take it you don't know any more about the provenance and dissemination of that document except what you believe you can glean from the document itself?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can go, Mr. Thompson, to the -- really, the very end of your report, page 19, the penultimate page. The last paragraph beginning on that page you begin: "As noted by Serbian analyst Branko Milinkovic quotes the great majority of the Serbian media deal with the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina generally within a rather stable matrix based on the following tenets: 1, Bosnia and Herzegovina is mentioned only with the prefix 'the former' or the 'so-called.' " Mr. Thompson, from your study of this material, do you -- in your opinion, was that objectionable?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It was prejudicial and -- Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time was internationally recognised as the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So to refer to it as the former or the so-called was intended to be prejudicial usage in order to confirm to the audience -- to the people -- to the consumers of those media outlets that it was former or only -- only former, not actual and only so-called, not real.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was a -- do you agree, it was an obvious corollary of the Bosnian Serb position in this continuing conflict, that they should label Bosnia and Herzegovina in that way?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: We're talking about the Serbian media here, not the Bosnian Serb leadership's discourse. Would you like me to clarify the distinction? The distinction is that it's not incumbent -- well, it's incumbent upon the Serbian media not simply to adopt the political discourse and labels used by one side in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's a separate question, Mr. Thompson.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I think it's an answer to your question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, do you agree it was an obvious corollary of the Bosnian Serb position in this continuing conflict that they should label Bosnia and Herzegovina in that way?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: It's a choice which was obvious from their point of view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And secondly, the conflict is a civil and ethnic war and not one of aggression. Now, first of all, Mr. Thompson, you would agree, would you, that the Bosnian Serb leadership, their position was a -- very plainly, that it was a civil war and not a war of aggression by them?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: That was their public position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you say that it was a war of aggression by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Do I say that it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, if you're asking me now, can I say that, the answer is: Yes, I can. I don't think it features in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that -- when did that first become your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we enter into the area of what is a war of aggression, I may remind you that since 1945 it took the United Nations until 1974 to define what aggression was. And when finally the Rome statute had to be established, then there was one portion of the rules and jurisdiction not operational, that was the jurisdiction over aggression. This Chamber and many Chambers in this Tribunal have heard many times the word "aggression" used or "aggressors" where reference was made to opponents. I would think that it's good, as you try to elicit from the witness to know what his position is as to who's to be blamed for starting this war or starting hostilities, I would rather not do that on the basis of the term war of aggression for the reasons I just mentioned. And I'm -- fully agree that we should try to find out about the position that the witness takes in this respect but rather than in other terms than the one you used. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in common with at least one of the members of the Bench, I was in Rome myself in July of 1998, so I do remember that point, Your Honour. May I say, Your Honour, that the phrase "one of aggression," in other words war of aggression, is one that appears in terms in the witness's report, which is what triggered off my question. But, Your Honour, the question and answer have been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find that -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And point 4 -- oh, I beg your pardon. The -- over the page, page 20 of your report, the sentence: "Croatian and Muslim forces are repeating all the atrocities they committed against the Serbian people during the Second World War." Mr. Thompson, you do know this much don't you, that there were atrocities on all sides during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then point 4: "All bodies and institutions within the international community, which are seen as a malevolent dragon with a hundred heads, from the European Union, the OSCE, and NATO right up to the UN itself have demonstrated that they have a biased attitude and are anti--Serbian." Mr. Thompson, it's correct, isn't it, the Bosnian Serbs, whether or not they were alone in that, the Bosnian Serbs deeply resented the German -- Germany's push for recognition of an independent Croatia, followed quickly thereafter by European Union support?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that they saw that as a biased pro-Croat/anti--Serb position, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, many of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's, for example, Lord Carrington, former foreign minister of the United Kingdom, was himself very strongly opposed and indeed dismayed by Germany's and then the consequent European Union position, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Can I point out that I'm quoting here from a Serbian analyst of probity and reputation and I'm quoting him because this passage provides a useful summary of the way in which Serbian media dealt with and framed their coverage of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So therefore I'm happy -- I regard that as a good summary. I'm happy to agree with it, but I would just like to point out that it's not my language. Now, yes, indeed, Lord Carrington was dismayed by the EU policy at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, are you then saying that in this whole passage and whole quote from the Serbian analyst -- it's my own language, isn't it -- in this whole quote from the Serbian analyst Branko Milenkovic, you are merely reporting what he says and you are not in any sense endorsing --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: I do agree with it, but I'm just -- I'm -- the questioning's not very clear to me, but I can keep -- I just wanted to remind the Court that this is not -- these are not my words. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understands this line of questioning, Mr. Thompson, to be the following: That where you've chosen to quote and to join the opinion of this analyst -- yes, of Mr. Milenkovic, that Mr. Stewart is now testing on the basis of other circumstances whether it was a right thing to do so. Isn't it -- did I understand you, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Thompson, the question is this: Did you, in your opinion, point 4, that the Bosnian Serbs through the -- or the Serbian media in presenting the view that those international -- or the international community had a biased attitude of anti-Serb, you find that point of view objectionable?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I find it partly understandable. You've pointed out one -- one reason why it would be partly understandable because of the policy decisions taken by the EU in the second half of December 1991 and so forth. But these -- it's a matter of degree, isn't it. Of course all bodies and institutions in the international community were not anti-Serbian. And the actions -- for example, the decisions and deployments of the United Nations would make no sense from that point of view. So partly understandable, but incorrect and tragically incorrect, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, is it understandable that at a time of conflict the Serbian media should present point 4 in the terms there summarised?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No, because it's throwing sand in the public's face. They are misleading the public as to the stands taken by international organisations and powerful states.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, don't -- for practical purposes, all governments and politicians who are involved in the operation and -- in some way operation and running of an armed conflict engage in manipulation and exaggeration of the strictly factual truth?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, temptation is bound to be there for any government engaged in such a high-risk policy, but the decision -- the actions taken by governments are not all alike and the behaviour of media in different countries are not all alike. And the Serbian government of course claimed not to be involved in the Bosnian war, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, given what you, at least the degree of acknowledgment in the answer you've just given, starting from a base of a -- well, in Serbia, starting from a base of a rather more captive media that is met in many western democracies, do you agree that it's hardly surprising that the politicians did succumb to that temptation?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, no. I wouldn't -- I wouldn't consent to that characterisation of the situation. The condition of the media in Serbia was very different, not only somewhat different, from the situation of media in western Europe at that time. And it's important to remember that the Serbian media were subjected to political control at this time to ensure that they were all -- all the key media outlets were disseminating the same message. So the level of pluralism and professionalism in the Serbian media was actually attacked and reduced by the political authorities in order to make sure that this single focussed set of messages went out to their own people and the Bosnian Serbs regarding their situation. I don't think that's normal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The level of pluralism and professionalism in the Serbian media was below the normal situation in western Europe before the SDS even came into existence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But there were -- at the end -- in the late 1980s and the turn of decade into the 1990s, there were attempts by liberal-minded journalists and -- to push back the boundaries of what was permissible to be said and to liberalise as far as they could. And those efforts were -- were stamped on by the Serbian regime. Not totally, but they were where they presented the real threat to the regime, namely where they were occurring in the most popular and broadly influential outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 17 of your report, just going back to that, talking about RTS you say, second line under heading 2, contents, you say: "Two analysts who examined coverage of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the six-week pre-election campaign in late 1992 concluded that "the horrors of war which could be seen in the reports on foreign TV stations were conspicuously absent." Now, Mr. Thompson, isn't that broadly similar, for example, to the United States' government wish for coffins for coffins returning from Iraq not to be seen on television by the American public?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: That's an interesting idea. I don't think there's a substantial analogy there at all. These were not -- this wasn't a matter of guidelines on taste and decency which become particularly political during times of war. This, in my view and the view of the analyst in question, was an attempt to mislead the public as to the nature of what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson --

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: To play down the terrible things that were happening and being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Thompson, the example I've given has nothing to do with taste and decency, has it? It's that the US government simply was unable in the end to prevent the American media from showing such things, and they would have done if they could. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: They weren't able to do it because there's media pluralism and because the entire political context is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you ask whether matters are similar, then of course the witness can say in what respect he sees differences. I think as a matter of fact that by saying these weren't guidelines on taste and decency, he would consider that in the other situation they were. But let's just proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is entirely entitled to -- as he answers the questions to answer them any way he likes and Your Honours can judge. Your Honour raises taste and decency --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So since you raise that, Mr. Thompson, taste and decency by the United States government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- by some of the photographs of Saddam Hussein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said "the example I have given has nothing to do with taste and decency," the witness made taste and decency part of his comparison and you invited him to compare the situations by asking whether they were similar or not. So therefore it's up to the witness to the witness to create a context of what he considers to be similar or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I challenged his answer at page 88, line 1, that's what I did, which is legitimate, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've received -- we've have an addendum to your report, Mr. Thompson, and it says: "Having examined the further material supplied to me on the 1st of June, 2005, I would like to draw attention to the following statements by Mr. Krajisnik as quoted in this material," and then you cite quite a lot of them. I'm not going to ask you questions about those specifically, Mr. Thompson. You say: "These statements and allegations conform to the patterns of media content described in my report." Can we just be clear that that further material was supplied to you on the 1st of June, 19 -- 2005 by the Office of the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was their selection of material supplied to you rather than yours?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, self-evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you do any further research around that material to find other or similar or related material?

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So effectively, the addendum to your report is a summary of what can be read in that material.

utterances.speaker: MARK THOMPSON
utterances.text: Well, it's what it is. It's what it states it is in the first sentence. It's an analysis of that further material in the sort of light of what I've -- of what is already written in the report, in the light of the priorities and the areas of concern and interest which are highlighted in the report. There's clearly more in that material, which is about 80 or 90 pages long, more than I've drawn attention to here. But this seemed the most salient content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thompson, you -- you've written, among other things, and I'm -- I -- I'm citing from something that was published in the Guardian Weekly, and I'm afraid I don't know whether it's the 5th of September or the 9th of May, because I don't know whether it's American or English dating, but it was in 2002.
